clue.text: Mostly welcome king from former European monarchy

indicators.note: mostly means most of the word for welcome is kept, its final letter dropped

parts.note: to welcome someone is to greet them
K is the chess and card abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A largely friendly reception for a king from a country no longer ruled by one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mostly' signals dropping the last letter of the welcome word; 'from former European monarchy' is adjectival, as in a Greek prince.
explanation.definitionFit: Greece was a kingdom until 1973, so something Greek comes from a former European monarchy.

clue.text: As amphibian, am found in sea and land, possibly? Right

indicators.note: possibly says the letters might be arranged some other way, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A riddle about an amphibian, at home in both sea and land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals the anagram; the 'and' between sea and land only joins the fodder, and the opening 'As' is a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A salamander is a tailed amphibian related to newts.

clue.text: Total acclamation in hall unfortunately followed by trouble

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong for the word hall, so its letters are jumbled

parts.note: to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Applause in a hall spoilt by some disturbance afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' signals the anagram, and 'followed by' puts the trouble word last; 'Total' looks like part of the wordplay but belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A greeting of wholehearted praise, as hailing a king; the phrase is an old cry of welcome.

clue.text: Old-fashioned royal entertainer, kind of sweet

definitions.meaning: a jester kept at a medieval court to amuse the monarch
a cold dessert of puréed fruit folded into cream, as in gooseberry

explanation.surface: A court jester described as a sort of confection.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a court jester and a creamy fruit pudding share this name.

clue.text: In a haar, with smew and tern at sea, unknown seabird

indicators.note: In tells us the unknown letter is placed inside the rearranged birds and mist
at sea means confused, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: X is the algebraic symbol for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: In a sea mist, among smews and terns, some unidentified seabird is seen.
explanation.walkthrough: A haar is a cold sea fog on Britain's east coast; 'at sea' signals the anagram, and 'In' puts the unknown inside it. The smew and tern are real birds used only for letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A black-and-white shearwater of the North Atlantic, named after the Isle of Man where it once bred.

clue.text: One emperor repelled follower of another

indicators.note: repelled means driven back, so the whole run of letters is read backwards

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article
a tsar was a Russian emperor

explanation.surface: An emperor is driven back by a supporter of a rival emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'repelled' turns A TSAR backwards. The other emperor is Haile Selassie of Ethiopia, revered by Rastafarians.
explanation.definitionFit: Rastafarians venerate the Ethiopian emperor Haile Selassie, so one is his follower.

clue.text: Stinks produced as nice cheese cart upset

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters of nice cheese cart are scattered

explanation.surface: A bad smell comes from an overturned cart of good cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges NICE CHEESE CART. 'Stinks' is old British schoolboy slang for chemistry, and so a nickname for the teacher of it.
explanation.definitionFit: In British public-school slang, chemistry was called stinks, a nickname extended to the master teaching it.

clue.text: Royal house's covers for crowns

definitions.meaning: belonging to the Scottish castle owned by the British royal family
round Scottish bonnets worn on top of a person's skull

explanation.surface: The royal residence keeps hats for its kings and queens.
explanation.definitionFit: Balmoral Castle is a royal residence in Aberdeenshire; a balmoral is also a flat Scottish cap.

clue.text: Reproduced single, without hit for so long

indicators.note: reproduced means copied, so the word for a single run is written twice

parts.note: in cricket a bye is a run scored when the batsman has not hit the ball

explanation.surface: A record is re-released, and still no chart hit.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, a bye is a run taken when the ball passes the batsman untouched, here 'single, without hit'; 'Reproduced' doubles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal ways of saying goodbye.

clue.text: So-called king dangerous woman cut short

indicators.note: cut short means the last letter of the word for a dangerous woman is lopped off

parts.note: a siren is a seductive and dangerous woman, after the singers of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A supposed king whose dangerous lover is cut down.
explanation.walkthrough: A king is called 'Sire' when addressed, hence 'So-called'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sire was the respectful form of address to a monarch.

clue.text: The blaze I put out for monarch

indicators.note: put out suggests a fire being extinguished and dispersed, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Extinguishing a fire for the sake of a queen.
explanation.definitionFit: Two English queens regnant bore this name.

clue.text: Not as strict as King Albert? Just the opposite

indicators.note: just the opposite says the order of King Albert is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: Rex is Latin for king
Al is a short form of Albert

explanation.surface: Is King Albert less strict? No, the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just the opposite' reads REX AL backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Lax means slack or lenient, and this is its comparative form.

clue.text: Why a distinguished 10 finds retirement difficult?

definitions.text: Why a distinguished 10 finds retirement difficult?

parts.words: Why a distinguished 10 finds retirement difficult?
parts.note: 10 is a queen named Elizabeth; retirement here means going to bed, and the clue asks why a monarch sleeps badly, answered by a line from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2

explanation.surface: An eminent monarch struggles to step down from her role.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retirement' suggests giving up the throne but means going to bed; the answer is Henry IV's line about why a king cannot sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's king laments sleeplessness as the burden of rule, so a monarch rests uneasily.

clue.text: Arranged a musical production and performed better than ever

parts.note: to set music is to arrange it for performance
a record is a recorded piece of music

explanation.surface: Someone arranged a musical show and outperformed every earlier effort.
explanation.definitionFit: To beat the best performance ever recorded is to establish a new best.

clue.text: See 12
See 12
Group of royals upper-class in origins

indicators.note: in tells us the upper-class letter sits within the word for origins

parts.note: starts are beginnings or origins
U is the old abbreviation for upper-class, as in U and non-U

explanation.surface: A royal group whose roots lie in the upper classes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stuarts were the dynasty ruling Scotland, and later England too, in the seventeenth century.

clue.text: King embracing lower classes as ruler

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic monarch
D and E are the lowest social grades in the British classification

explanation.surface: A king hugging the poor as their ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: British social grades run A, B, C1, C2, D and E, so the lowest are DE.
explanation.definitionFit: A leader is one who heads and governs, a ruler.

clue.text: See 12
One serving queen, as member of exclusive group initially formed

definitions.meaning: a worker insect tending its colony's queen

definitions.text: member of exclusive group initially formed
definitions.meaning: a White Anglo-Saxon Protestant, a term formed from initial letters for a privileged American elite

explanation.surface: A royal servant is also part of a select club from the start.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a stinging insect serving its queen and the acronym for a White Anglo-Saxon Protestant.

clue.text: Exemplary worker supporting English king and US president

indicators.note: in a down answer, supporting means placed underneath, so the worker comes after

parts.note: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George
the ant is the proverbial model of industry

explanation.surface: A hardworking person backs an English king and an American president.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer 'supporting' puts ANT below GR.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses S. Grant was the eighteenth US president.

clue.text: Course of royalty for one such as King James

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article
James VI was King of Scotland before also gaining England's throne

explanation.surface: A royal racecourse suits someone like King James.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Ascot is a racecourse in Berkshire with a famous royal race meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: The racecourse hosts Royal Ascot, attended annually by the monarch.

clue.text: Old rock band appearing West End before king

indicators.note: before places the first piece ahead of the word for king
End here picks out the final letter of West

parts.note: Rex is Latin for king

explanation.surface: A veteran rock group plays London's West End ahead of royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like London's theatre district, but 'End' takes the last letter of 'West'.
explanation.definitionFit: T. Rex was Marc Bolan's glam rock band of the 1970s.

clue.text: A British tyrant has little time to oust former ruler

indicators.note: to oust is to throw out, so one letter is removed from the tyrant

parts.note: a dictator is an absolute ruler, a tyrant
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A British despot loses no time getting rid of a deposed leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to oust' takes T out of DICTATOR, leaving DICATOR.
explanation.definitionFit: One who abdicates gives up the throne and is thereafter a one-time monarch.

clue.text: Person who formally introduces current monarch

parts.note: present means current, happening now
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

explanation.surface: Someone who makes formal introductions of the reigning queen.
explanation.definitionFit: A presenter is one who introduces people or a programme.

clue.text: Again show one Tudor or another, as placed in succession

indicators.note: placed in says one piece is put inside the other

parts.note: a run is a succession or unbroken series
ER, a royal cipher, fits Edward VI or Elizabeth I, both Tudors

explanation.surface: Tudor monarchs follow one another in line of succession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'succession' looks like the royal line but is just a run.
explanation.definitionFit: To rerun a programme is to broadcast it once more.
